newsitem.title: GERMANY: Toepfer oilseeds study stresses soybean dependency.
newsitem.headline: Toepfer oilseeds study stresses soybean dependency.

text.p: Tight world oilseeds markets in the 1996/97 season depended on higher soybean supplies to make up for shortfalls in commodities replaced by lucrative grains, grain trader Alfred C Toepfer wrote in a study on Friday.
Major importer China was likely to require soybeans before the arrival of Latin American crops in early 1997 and this underlined the role of the U.S. as the most important supplier.
"This strongly suggests prices in the international soya market will remain highly volatile over the next few months," Toepfer said.
Global oilseeds output in 1996/97 was estimated at 255 million tonnes, broadly steady on the 95/96 season.
But the share of soybeans rose to 52 percent at 133 million from 48 percent and 124 million tonnes respectively.
Rapeseed, cotton seed, sun seed, copra, palmkernel and groundnut output was cut mostly amid competition from grain.
The Oct 11 USDA soy crop estimate for the U.S., which was up eight percent at 63.9 million tonnes, resulted in price falls in the Chicago soya complex over the past week.
Toepfer said the price declines as a result of volume pressure could bottom out if U.S. soybean crushings turned out higher than assumed.
While USDA had estimated a 37.4 million tonne crush for 96/97, just 100,000 tonnes above 95/96, this figure could rise if demand in export markets expanded.
Latin American growers were already beginning to run out of old crop supplies and domestic U.S. demand may also rise.
World market prices in the second half of the 96/97 season hinged on the pace and size of Brazilian and Argentinian shipments, which to date looked set to be ample.
But equally important would be Chinese import patterns.
